t: How To Give Your Students Unforgettable Directions
q: Your students will pay close attention if you make your directions sound like a story progressing from beginning to end.

Going to” is a memory device that causes students to create a moving picture in their mind. It’s also predictive. They take it as fact that they’ll indeed be able to do everything you ask them—without your help.

Silly tasks like this act as anchors along a memory map for your students. The novelty and goofiness has a way of helping them remember the path that leads from the beginning of the activity to the successful end.
By being proactive and asking if anyone doesn’t understand, you effectively put the onus of speaking up on your students—saddling them with a greater feeling of responsibility to do it right.

Many teachers place giving individual help at the top of their priority list and don’t give a second thought to how they provide the directions—which creates needy, dependent students whose first inclination is to look to their teacher rather than relying on themselves.
x: Using the phrase 'going to' throughout directions is described as a memory device that prompts students to visualize themselves completing each step.

t: The One Thing Standing In Your Way Of Having Your Dream Class ng-your-dream-class/
q: The one thing standing in your way of creating the class you’ve always wanted is believing that you can.
You must first visualize your goal before in can become a reality. Keep a sharp image of your perfect class in your mind’s eye and review it daily—both before and after school.
Indulging in failures and disappointments and conjuring up justifications is as effortless as slipping into a warm bath.
The staff lounge is a dangerous place. The old adage that you should avoid it is spot on.
We didn’t get into teaching to snivel about students, complain with colleagues, or gin up excuses for ourselves. We got in it to make a difference.
x: Linsin argues that belief, not circumstance, is the single biggest obstacle to building the classroom a teacher wants, and offers a practical process for building that belief.

t: Why You Should Take Your Time Responding To Misbehavior
q: It’s best to observe from a short distance, responding only after the misbehavior has played itself out.

If you get involved too soon, it will be a challenge sorting through what happened and who is deserving of a consequence. Confusion is a difficult student’s best friend, and by diving in too quickly, you’ll be swimming in a sea of denials, arguments, and accusations.
A delayed response gives your students a chance to think twice about their misbehavior. In fact, your observing presence all but forces them to make a choice.
Interrupting misbehavior is personal, for both them and you—making it easy to lose your composure, raise your voice, say things you’ll regret, and incite anger and pushback from your students.
They know that if they misbehave on your watch, there is no arguing, finger pointing, or clever misdirection. Just consequences.
x: Linsin challenges the instinct to interrupt misbehavior the moment it starts, arguing that observing from a short distance and responding only after it plays out is more effective.
Interrupting misbehavior too quickly is identified as a common but counterproductive instinct that creates confusion about what actually happened.
A delayed response gives students a window to self-correct and take responsibility for their own behavior before the teacher steps in.
